1.pericope_label: The command to raise a memorial

schools.summary: Gill is content to date the moment, when all the people were clean passed over. Calvin warns that the order of telling is not the order of events: what is interposed should be read as a pluperfect, since the stones were lifted from beside the priests' feet before those feet moved, and the setting of them up at Gilgal came afterwards. On why the command came from God rather than from Joshua he answers from effect: had Joshua raised a trophy of that kind of his own accord, the piety that dictated it might have been laudable enough, but an admonition founded only on the will of man might perhaps have been despised, whereas when God himself raises the sign, it is impious to pass it carelessly by.

Henry begins with what the chapter interrupts. Besides marching into an enemy's country in the face of the enemy, they had wives and children and families, cattle and tents, bag and baggage, to convey by a strange and untrodden path, muddy or stony, troublesome to the weak and frightful to the timorous, with a steep descent to the bottom of the river and a steep ascent out of it — every man with his head full of care and his hands full of business, and Joshua more than any of them. And yet in the midst of all that hurry the memorial had to be seen to, and the care of it might not be adjourned to a time of greater leisure: however much we have to do of business for ourselves and our families, we must not omit what we have to do for the glory of God, for that is our best business. He answers the same question Calvin does, but from appearance rather than effect — had Joshua done it without divine direction it might have looked like a design to perpetuate his own name and honour, and would not have commanded so venerable a regard from posterity. And he gives a candid reason for needing the sign at all: some of the Israelites were so little affected by the mercy that they felt no concern to have it remembered, while others were so deeply affected that they thought no memorial could be needed, since the heart and tongue of every Israelite in every age would be a living monument of it; God, knowing their frame and how apt they had been to forget his works, provided for both. On the bearers he notes that one man came out of each tribe, so that each might have the story told them by one of their own, the two tribes already settled in their possession lending a hand to the memorial of a mercy they shared.
Wesley notes only that the order is not new but a repetition with enlargement of what had been commanded before, now to be put in execution.

Keil notices a mark in the text itself, the piska standing in the middle of the first verse, an old pre-Masoretic sign that the Masorites left in place, indicating a space and showing that a new section began there. He gives the command its full form, that the twelve were to go before the ark into the midst of Jordan and take every man a stone upon his shoulder from the standing-place of the priests, carry them over, and lay them down in the place of encampment where they should lodge that night.

debates.question: Why did the command to raise the memorial come from God rather than from Joshua?

positions.position: otherwise it would have looked like a design to perpetuate Joshua's own name, and would not have commanded so venerable a regard
an admonition founded only on the will of man might have been despised; when God raises the sign it is impious to pass it by

outliers.note: reads a scribal mark rather than the narrative — the piska mid-verse, left standing by the Masorites, showing where an older division of the text began

themes: business for God amid business for ourselves
why the sign was needed at all

2.pericope_label: Twelve stones taken up, and twelve set in the river

schools.summary: Gill takes the stones set in the river to have been twelve others, on the authority of the Greek and Latin versions and of Jarchi, piled one upon another so as to stand above the water; and since the water of Jordan is clear, they could be made out by anyone crossing or walking the bank. He adds a guess worth having, that these may be the very stones John the Baptist pointed at, since he baptized at Bethabara, supposed to be the place of the crossing and named from it. Calvin makes the most of the stated purpose: though the stones cannot speak, the monument furnished the parents with materials for speaking, and with the means of making God's kindness known to their children; zeal for propagating piety is required of the aged, since it was God's will that the doctrine should be handed down through every age, so that those not yet born might become witnesses to it by hearing. He notices why the number matched the tribes, that each might be incited to gratitude by its own symbol, and answers the objection that the two and a half tribes had no need of the passage — the land was possessed for the common good of the whole race of Abraham, and men engaged in a common cause are not to be separated. On the submerged stones he concedes the difficulty rather than arguing it away: there was apparently no use in stones under the water, and a monument altogether buried in silence would indeed have been useless, but when the people talked among themselves of the evidence left down there, the hearing of what they could not see strongly confirmed their faith — as the ark itself was shut behind a veil, and its hidden splendour was not without benefit to those who knew from the Law what lay inside.

Clarke reports Kennicott's objection in full: is it likely the memorial should be erected in the very place from which the stones were taken, where, when the river reunited, it would be concealed and could be no memorial at all? Kennicott's solution was to emend the preposition, reading from the midst rather than in the midst. Clarke will not have it, the reading being unsupported by a single copy in his own collection or De Rossi's, though between them they amount to four hundred and ninety-four; he holds instead that a base of strong stonework may have raised the stones high enough to remain visible. Wesley argues the same case from size, that these were not the stones a man could carry on his shoulder but much larger ones set in two rows, visible at least when the water was low; and he reads the choice of one man per tribe as the surest means of spreading the report of the work among them all.

Ellicott solves the difficulty by the idiom. In the midst of Jordan does not mean what an English reader hears; with the river divided, half recoiling northward and the rest running away south, a man standing between the two parts stands in the midst of Jordan whether he is at the edge of the water or not — and the Hebrew phrase need mean no more than within, as Simeon's inheritance was within Judah's while lying entirely along one edge of it. He takes two cairns to have been set up, one on either side, the western at Gilgal and the other at the edge of the overflow where the priests had stopped, and calls it contrary to common sense as well as to the text to suppose a cairn was built in the river's bed. Keil is careful with the verb, since the men laid the stones down in the place of encampment, and the setting of them up at Gilgal is not mentioned until later.

debates.question: How could stones set in the midst of Jordan serve as a memorial?

positions.position: they stood high enough to be seen — piled up, or raised on a base of stonework, and visible through clear or low water
the phrase does not mean mid-channel; the cairn stood at the edge of the overflow, where the priests halted
they were indeed submerged, and worked by report rather than by sight — as the ark did behind its veil

outliers.note: answers a conjectural emendation with a manuscript count, refusing Kennicott's reading because not one of the four hundred and ninety-four copies he and De Rossi collated supports it

themes: stones for the children to ask about
a memorial no one could see
what “in the midst of Jordan” means

10.pericope_label: The priests standing, and the people hasting over

schools.summary: Gill notes that the priests stood in the midst of Jordan, though on dry ground, the waters being divided. Calvin, who knows how hard the standing was, works it out: if we are ordered to halt while others are hastening, a feeling of irksomeness is easily produced, because we seem to occupy an inferior position — and the priests had more than that to bear, since they might well have begun to doubt whether the heaps of water suspended over their heads would hold. They showed their piety no less by remaining there than by venturing into the current in the first place: the going in proved their ready obedience, the standing still proved their constancy, and made it plain that they had not obeyed from a mere impulse, since firmness of that kind must have its origin in a living principle. On the clause about what Moses commanded he offers a division of labour — Moses had carefully enjoined Joshua to hang upon the lips of God, so that the command of Moses was general while God gave special injunctions as each circumstance arose.

Henry finds four different motives in the same hurry. Some hasted because they were not able to trust God, afraid the waters would return, being conscious of guilt and diffident of the divine power; others because they were unwilling to tempt God by continuing the miracle longer than needs must, or to stretch the patience of the priests who bore the ark; others because they were eager to be in Canaan and would show how much they longed for that pleasant land; and those who considered least of all hasted because everyone else was hasting. His verdict is the sentence to keep: he that believeth doth not make haste to anticipate God's counsels, but he makes haste to attend them. On what Moses commanded he takes it for the general instruction rather than a particular order, the thing being altogether new to Joshua, and what Moses had charged him with was to follow the divine direction and deliver to the people what he received of the Lord — instructions given by a man now dead and gone, which Joshua had ready when the occasion came, as it is well for us to have ours.

Clarke takes the haste as a mark of authenticity: how very natural the circumstance is, since men seeing the waters divided and the river running back would naturally fear it might resume its course at any moment — and the fact that such a detail is recorded at all is a proof that the relater was an eyewitness of the passage. Wesley reads the haste more simply, as an argument of their fear or of the weakness of their faith, and points the contrast with the priests, who are commended for standing firm and settled in their minds as well as in the posture of their bodies.

Ellicott alone leans toward taking the clause about Moses literally, thinking it would seem that the crossing had been the subject of some directions by Moses, though nothing is written of the manner of it in the Pentateuch. And he adds a reflection the others do not reach for: had Israel gone up when Moses brought them to the frontier at Kadesh-barnea in the second year, they would have had no occasion to cross the Jordan at all, and when the route was changed we cannot say.

debates.question: What had Moses commanded Joshua concerning the crossing?

positions.position: nothing particular — only the general charge to follow divine direction and deliver what he received from the Lord
it would seem there were actual directions from Moses about the passage, though nothing of the manner survives in the Pentateuch

outliers.note: treats the people's haste as internal evidence of authorship — a detail too incidental to invent, and therefore a sign that the narrator was present

themes: the harder obedience of standing still
what Moses had commanded about this

11.pericope_label: The forty thousand, and Joshua magnified

schools.summary: Gill puts the number liable at a hundred and thirty thousand, of whom Joshua took only about forty thousand select men, the rest left to their flocks and lands; and on the magnifying of Joshua he says simply that God made him great and honourable in their esteem by doing what he had foretold. Calvin decides the question of the agreement on grounds of humanity. It may probably be conjectured that Moses never meant to insist strictly that every man who had assented should leave his wife and children and serve until Canaan was wholly subdued; it would have been harsh and cruel to leave an unwarlike multitude unprotected in the midst of many hostile nations, and the remains of the enemy, helped by their neighbours, would not long have failed to take such an opportunity of massacring the women and children. Moses was not of so stern a nature as not to consult for the helpless, nor would his prudence have left a territory lately seized by arms unoccupied by troops; and so immense a concourse would in any case have impeded the taking of Canaan rather than assisted it. All he required was that the Reubenites and Gadites should not remain indolently at home, eating their food at ease, while their brethren carried on the war. Calvin then praises the forty thousand for what they did not say: they might readily have alleged that they were as well entitled to exemption as the rest, and instead they went with alacrity once the levy was made, without envying their brethren the immunity. On Joshua being magnified he is careful about the order of things — it was not the principal end of the miracle to proclaim his pre-eminence, but since it greatly concerned the public interest that his government should be firmly established, this is justly set down as a further instance of divine favour, for a promiscuous multitude not ruled by a head falls apart of its own accord. He also meets the obvious objection, that the people plainly did not always fear Joshua, by observing that what is described is a settled government of the kind that came only after the turbulent generation had died and a better race succeeded.

Clarke refers the numbers of those who stayed behind to guard the families and cattle to his note on the earlier passage, where they amount to seventy thousand five hundred and eighty. Wesley reads the phrase before the Lord as meaning in the presence of a God who was watching whether they would keep the covenant made with their brethren.

Ellicott works from the last census — Reuben forty-three thousand seven hundred and thirty, Gad forty thousand five hundred, half Manasseh twenty-six thousand three hundred and fifty — giving a possible force of a hundred and ten thousand, so that more than half were left behind to protect their families and dwellings; and he judges this not inconsistent with the spirit of the agreement, since permission to build cities implies the right to fortify and defend them. He also asks, without answering, why Reuben and Gad discarded Simeon, their old companion in the order of march, and associated themselves with part of Manasseh. On the last verse he marks where the section ends and what it establishes: Joshua's standing as equal to Moses in the people's respect dates from the crossing of Jordan, which he thinks not to be forgotten in considering his Antitype. Keil explains why the notice comes in here at all — it is a supplement, inserted because no earlier place suited it, and yet it needed saying expressly that those tribes had performed the promise they gave, and in what manner; and he is careful that the wording not be misread as putting the forty thousand behind the priests with the ark, since the ark was the medium of the division.

debates.question: Did sending only forty thousand keep the promise made to Moses?

positions.position: yes in spirit — leaving families unguarded among hostile nations would have been cruel, and Moses required only that they not stay home at ease
yes, and consistently with the agreement as Joshua and Israel read it, since leave to build cities implies leave to defend them

outliers.note: answers the charge that the people never really feared Joshua by conceding it for the wilderness years and confining the verse to the settled obedience that followed the death of the murmuring generation

themes: forty thousand out of a hundred and more
the promise to Moses, kept in the letter or the spirit
why Joshua had to be magnified

15.pericope_label: The priests come up, and the waters return

schools.summary: Gill notices a change of title: everywhere before in this history the ark has been called the ark of the covenant, and here it is the ark of the testimony — which comes to the same thing, since the law was both the covenant between God and the people and a testimony of his will to them, and the Greek version uses both words. Calvin marks what the priests did not do, since they did not move a foot until Joshua gave the signal, and finds the same fatherly kindness in God's condescending to direct almost every step of their progress by his own voice, lest any perplexity should retard them. On the return of the water he draws the inference: had the river not returned to its former state, and suddenly, many would have imagined the cause of the change to be something hidden but fortuitous; but when God displays his power and favour at such minute intervals of time, all doubt is removed. Thus the river, though dumb, was the best of heralds, proclaiming with a loud voice that heaven and earth are subject to the God of Israel.

Clarke sets the two moments side by side: as soon as the soles of the priests' feet touched the water the stream was cut off, the course of the river continued inverted the whole time they stood in the channel, and as soon as their soles touched dry land again the waters immediately resumed their natural course — all of it done by the sovereign influence of the God whose presence the ark represented. Wesley notes that the priests stayed contentedly in the river until God by Joshua called them out, and catches the exactness of the wording, since being in the middle and deepest part they are most properly said to go up to the land.

Ellicott asks why the withdrawal of the priests is given a section of its own. It need not have been, for the purposes of the mere historical narrative — we might have taken it for granted that they came out — but the significance of the event was marked enough to earn a separate notice. We are not suffered to forget by what means Jordan was driven back and held in check, and the check was not meant to be perpetual: the suspension of the power of death for men has its limits, and when the day of grace is over the waters will return unto their place and flow over all the banks as before. Keil describes the moment in the Hebrew's own terms, the soles of the priests' feet tearing themselves loose from the soft soil of the river bed and treading upon firm ground, whereupon the waters returned and went over all the banks as they had done before — which he takes as saying as clearly as possible that it was the ark which held the stream back.

outliers.note: reads the separate notice of the priests' withdrawal as deliberate — the river was held back only while the ark stood there, and the waters returning is part of what the sign means, not merely the end of it

themes: obedience that waits for the word
the timing as proof of the miracle
a check that was never meant to be permanent

19.pericope_label: Gilgal, the twelve stones pitched, and the children's question

schools.summary: Gill reads the closing purpose widely, that the heathen at large would acknowledge the hand of the Lord when they saw the stones and were told their meaning, since the event was above the power of nature to effect. Calvin notes that Gilgal is named by anticipation, the name being given later at the renewal of circumcision, and argues backwards from the children's question to the arrangement of the stones: had they been heaped at random without order, it would never have come into the mind of posterity to inquire what they meant, so there must have been something remarkable enough in their position that the sight could not be overlooked. He then explains why the parents' answer works at all. Because the covenant ran unbroken through the generations, a mercy shown to the fathers belongs to the children by the unity of the body: had the favour been confined to a single day the parents' answer would have been coldly heard, but hearing that the waters were dried up ages before they were born, the sons' sons own themselves the people to whom it was shown. The same holds of the Red Sea, for of those who came out of Egypt only Caleb and Joshua survived, and yet Joshua addresses the whole people as if they had seen it — God dried up the Red Sea before our face — in virtue of an adoption passing without interruption from the fathers to the children.

Henry takes the stones to have been set either one upon another, yet so that they could be distinctly counted, or side by side in rows, and notes that once fixed they are not called a heap of stones but these stones. He makes the children's question the lesson: those that will be wise when they are old must be inquisitive when they are young, and our Lord, though he had in himself the fulness of knowledge, taught children by his own example to hear and ask questions. He observes that the place itself would serve as a memorandum, so that not only the inhabitants but strangers and travellers would look on the stones and receive instruction — many on seeing them would go to their Bibles and read the history, and some, reading the history at a distance, would have the curiosity to go and see the stones. And he states what all such instruction is for: in all the informations parents give their children they should have this chiefly in their eye, to teach and engage them to fear God for ever, since serious godliness is the best learning.

Clarke counts the date out — they left Egypt on the fifteenth of the first month and entered Canaan on the tenth of the first month forty years later, so that forty years wanting five days had elapsed — and supplies the etymology of Gilgal, that the root signifies to roll and the doubled form rolling off or away, before listing what the place became: the first camp in the land, the site of the circumcision and of the first passover kept in Canaan, Joshua's fortified base through the war, the place where Saul was proclaimed, where the manna ceased, and where the ark stood until the conquest was over. He thinks a base of mason-work was raised to a considerable height with the twelve set on top, since stones such as a man could carry would scarcely make an observable pillar. On the closing purpose he narrows the phrase, taking all the people of the earth to mean all the people of this land, the Canaanitish nations among whom the miracles were wrought; and he turns the verse on the reader's own household — a spirit of inquiry is common to every child, the human heart ever panting after knowledge, and if not rightly directed when young it will go astray after forbidden science, so when a child asks what you mean by this baptism, or by praying, the parent is handed an opportunity to teach every article of the faith. Wesley marks the same date and draws from it that so punctual is God in performing his word, whether promised or threatened, adding that the day fell very seasonably for the taking up of the lambs to be used four days after.

Ellicott observes that exactly forty years before, on the tenth day of the first month, Israel had been commanded to take a lamb for a house that they might keep the Passover; the forty years of the Exodus were now complete, and on the self-same day they passed the last barrier and entered the promised land. Keil states the double intention of the miracle as a pair: to reveal to the Canaanites the omnipotence of the God of Israel, the strong hand of the Lord, and to serve the Israelites as an impulse to fear the Lord their God always.

debates.question: Who are 'all the people of the earth' that were to know the hand of the Lord?

positions.position: the Canaanite nations in whose sight the miracles were wrought — all the people of this land
the heathen at large, who would acknowledge it when they heard what the stones meant

outliers.note: imagines the memorial working in both directions — travellers who see the stones going to their Bibles for the history, and readers of the history travelling to see the stones

themes: a monument arranged to be asked about
mercy to the fathers reckoned to the children
